_meta.purpose: Furniture that changes a room's function without changing the room. This is the STUFF layer doing adaptability, and it is the cheapest adaptability there is: no demolition, no carbon, no permit, measured in seconds rather than weeks.
_meta.why_this_matters_here: The project's thesis is usually argued at the space_plan layer — demountable partitions, movable walls. This dataset is the layer below it. A studio with a fold-away bed is literally a different room by day and by night, and the engine can test BOTH states against the standards. A plan that works deployed and fails stowed is not a flexible plan.
_meta.modelling_note: Each item carries two footprints. `deployed` is the in-use size; `stowed` is what it occupies the rest of the time. The clearance an item needs applies to its DEPLOYED state; the circulation it frees up applies to its stowed state. Testing only one state is how convertible furniture gets credited for flexibility it does not deliver.
_meta.source: Neufert, Architects' Data, 3rd English ed., printed p.158 (Rooms / Living Areas).
_meta.verification: Read directly from the rendered page 2026-10-06.

reference_bed_sizes.neufert_ref: p.158 figs.1,3,4 — 900 x 2000 mm is the recurring single bed; mattress widths run 900-2000 mm

items.name: Sofa bed, bedding stored in the covers
items.neufert_ref: p.158 fig.5 — sofa bed 2.00 m long, 800 mm deep as a sofa; duvet and pillows roll up during the daytime and zip into the covers
items.note: Storing the bedding inside the sofa is the detail that decides whether it gets used daily. Without it the bedding needs a cupboard, and the flexibility costs floor area somewhere else.

items.name: Sofa bed with pull-out mattress unit
items.neufert_ref: p.158 figs.8,14 — sofa bed (fold-out), 1.60 m deep deployed from 700 mm stowed, 1.90 m long

items.name: Armchair bed, fold-out
items.neufert_ref: p.158 fig.13 — armchair bed (fold-out), 1.40 m stowed to 2.00 m deployed; a separate container is required for the bedding
items.note: Neufert flags the bedding container explicitly. Flexibility that displaces storage has not removed the requirement, only moved it.

items.name: Frankfurt bed, folds away sideways
items.neufert_ref: p.158 fig.15 — Frankfurt bed folding away sideways, 1.10 m high cupboard, 2.00 x 900 mm deployed
items.note: Frees the entire bed footprint plus its 1.20-1.50 m access zone. In a studio that is the difference between a room that can hold a table and one that cannot.

items.name: Frankfurt bed, folds away vertically
items.neufert_ref: p.158 fig.16 — Frankfurt bed folding away vertically, 2.00 m high, 950 mm wide stowed; two adjacent units form a double bed

items.name: Cupboard-bed with clothes cupboard beneath
items.neufert_ref: p.158 fig.10 — cupboard-bed with low cupboard for clothes, 1.50 m high, 2.00 x 800 mm; suitable for very small rooms, ship's cabins and studio rooms
items.note: Does not fold away — it stacks sleeping on top of storage. A different strategy: it buys storage rather than floor area, and the floor stays committed.

items.name: High bed with deep drawers and slide-out board
items.neufert_ref: p.158 fig.9 — high bed with deep drawers and a slide-out board on top, 1.10 m high, 2.00 x 900 mm

items.name: Fold-up bed on rollers, stored in a cupboard
items.neufert_ref: p.158 figs.17,18 — fold-up bed on rollers for one or two people, rolled into a cupboard during the daytime; wall cupboard 1.50 m with a narrow door opening, 720 + 680 mm
items.note: The largest ratio of deployed to stowed footprint here, and the only one that can leave the room entirely — which makes the cupboard, not the bed, the thing to design.

items.name: Three-level bunks
items.neufert_ref: p.158 fig.11 — three-level bunks for dormobiles, weekend houses and children's rooms; space required 0.338 m2 per bed
items.note: 0.338 m2 per bed is the densest sleeping provision in the reference, and a useful floor for any density argument — it is what space costs when comfort is not the objective.
